title: DHCP Systems Engineering: Infrastructure Triage
subject: DHCP
description: In an enterprise network, DHCP is more than just 'handing out IPs.' It is a coordinated dance of broadcasts, relays, and Active Directory security checks. In this activity, you will troubleshoot lease failures across VLAN boundaries, resolve authorization blocks, and mitigate IP conflicts using professional diagnostic tools.
reportOverview: This report evaluates your ability to troubleshoot the DORA process and relay architecture. Use these results to refine your understanding of how DHCP interacts with Routers and Active Directory.
evidenceInstructions:
Instructions:
1) Analyze the symptom and artifacts (Event Logs, Packet Captures, Console Icons).
2) Select the Triage action that provides the most visibility into the hidden error.
3) Choose the Diagnosis that explains the logic of the failure.
4) Select the Fix that remediates the root cause based on industry standards.

tickets.title: Service Status: 'Running' but Console is Red
tickets.summary: A secondary DHCP server (DC-02) has been installed to provide redundancy. The service is 'Started' in Services.msc, but the DHCP console shows a red down arrow, and it is not responding to any client requests.
artifact: Console: IPv4 node shows a red down arrow icon
Event Viewer: System Log shows Event ID 1046: 'The DHCP service has determined that it is not authorized to service clients.'
validations: Verify server appears in 'Authorized Servers' list.
Test client lease acquisition via NV-CL1.

debrief.summary: In an AD environment, DHCP servers must be authorized in the directory before they can start leasing. This is a security feature to prevent 'Rogue DHCP' servers from disrupting the network. Even if the service is 'Running,' it will remain dormant until authorized.
debrief.takeaway: Always check Authorization status for new DHCP servers in AD. A 'Running' service does not mean an 'Active' service.

triage.q: The service is 'Running' in Windows, but the DHCP console is red. What is the most professional next step to identify why the server is dormant?
options: Restart the server to clear the icon
Check the System Event Log for Event ID 1046 (Authorization check)
Uninstall and reinstall the DHCP role
Change the service logon account to 'Domain Admin'

diagnosis.q: Event 1046 indicates the server is not authorized. What does this mean in a Domain environment?
options: The server has an expired license
The DHCP server's computer account is not in the 'DHCP Administrators' group
The server has not been whitelisted in Active Directory to provide DHCP services
The server's IP address is already in use by another device

fix.q: How do you resolve this 'Unauthorized' state in the DHCP management console?
options: Right-click the server node in the DHCP console and select 'Authorize'
Run 'gpupdate /force' on the Domain Controller
Assign a static IP address to the client machines
Reboot the primary Domain Controller

tickets.title: Remote Branch: APIPA 169.254.x.x Addresses
tickets.summary: Users in the new 'VLAN 20' subnet are unable to get an IP. They are receiving 169.254 addresses. The DHCP server is in 'VLAN 10' and is working fine for local users.
artifact: Router: Inter-VLAN routing is enabled; Branch users can ping HQ servers if they use static IPs.
DHCP Server: Scope for 172.18.2.0 is active and authorized.
validations: Verify DHCP Discover packets reach the server from VLAN 20.
Check Router configuration for IP Helper-Address.

debrief.summary: DHCP 'Discover' packets are Layer 2 broadcasts. Since routers block broadcasts, requests from VLAN 20 never reach the server in VLAN 10. A 'Relay Agent' (IP Helper) is required to convert that broadcast into a unicast packet.
debrief.takeaway: If routing works for static IPs but DHCP fails across subnets, the issue is almost always a missing Relay Agent or IP Helper configuration on the router.

triage.q: Clients in the remote subnet are getting APIPA addresses. What is the first thing you should check to see if the server is receiving their requests?
options: Check if the server's local firewall is blocking all UDP traffic
Perform a packet capture (Wireshark) on the DHCP server to see if 'DHCP Discover' packets are arriving from the 172.18.2.0 gateway
Check the 'Address Leases' for the local HQ subnet
Verify the server has enough RAM to handle more requests

diagnosis.q: Static IPs can communicate across VLANs, but DHCP captures show zero traffic from the remote subnet. What is the logical failure?
options: The DHCP server is too slow to respond to remote clients
The Router/Gateway for VLAN 20 is not configured to relay DHCP broadcasts to the server's IP
The DHCP server needs a physical network card in every VLAN
The scope for 172.18.2.0 has a typo in the subnet mask

fix.q: What is the industry-standard remediation for this multi-subnet architecture?
options: Configure an 'IP Helper-Address' (DHCP Relay) on the VLAN 20 gateway interface pointing to the DHCP server IP
Create a 'Superscope' on the DHCP server to merge the two subnets
Increase the lease duration to 30 days to reduce broadcast traffic
Enable 'Promiscuous Mode' on the DHCP server's network adapter

tickets.title: Scope Flooded with 'BAD_ADDRESS'
tickets.summary: The DHCP console for the NewVue_Internal scope is filling up with 'BAD_ADDRESS' entries. Users are reporting intermittent 'IP Address Conflict' popups on their workstations.
artifact: Console: 15 'BAD_ADDRESS' entries appear in the lease list.
Context: A team recently installed 10 smart-sensors with manual static IPs in the middle of the dynamic range.
Server Properties: 'Conflict Detection Attempts' is set to 2.
validations: Identify the static IP range used by the sensors.
Create exclusions for those IPs in the DHCP scope.
Clear BAD_ADDRESS entries and verify they do not return.

debrief.summary: The DHCP server uses 'Conflict Detection' to ping an IP before offering it to a client. If it gets a response (meaning a device is already using that IP statically), it marks it 'BAD_ADDRESS' and moves to the next IP. This prevents the server from causing a conflict.
debrief.takeaway: BAD_ADDRESS is a symptom of a 'Rogue' static IP or a missing exclusion. Use Exclusions to protect any IPs that are manually assigned to devices.

triage.q: You see 'BAD_ADDRESS' in the lease list. What does this tell you about the DHCP server's internal logic?
options: The DHCP database is corrupted and needs a repair
The server attempted to issue an IP but detected a conflict via ICMP (Ping) before completing the lease
The clients have invalid MAC addresses
The server has run out of available IP addresses

diagnosis.q: Why are these conflicts occurring if the DHCP server is 'aware' of them?
options: The DHCP server is malfunctioning
Devices are being manually assigned static IPs that fall within the dynamic 'Address Pool' without an Exclusion record
The lease duration is too short, causing clients to fight for IPs
The DNS server is not updating PTR records fast enough

fix.q: What is the best way to prevent 'BAD_ADDRESS' entries from re-appearing?
options: Disable Conflict Detection to speed up leasing
Configure an 'Address Exclusion' range that covers the IPs used by the static devices
Tell the users to reboot their machines until the error goes away
Increase the range of the scope so there are 'more' IPs available
